notes: Ruling slot 10 = House of Thani as a Wahhabi monarchy (Ahmad bin Ali), matching MD's pro-Saudi Al Thani entry. MD's second House of Thani (slot 13) replaced by the Heir Apparent Khalifa bin Hamad's administration, the real power centre in 1970. Slot 23 holds the Al Thani allowance-holders (dynastic privilege bloc) so the house is not duplicated. National Unity Front (1963, banned) in 20 and Ba'ath in 21 as in MD; Muslim Brotherhood network (Qaradawi) in 12; Fatah's Doha branch in 18; ANM in 5 and PFLOAG (Maoist-influenced) in 19.

0.name: British Political Agency in Qatar
0.text:
Under the Anglo-Qatari treaty of 1916 Britain conducts Qatar's foreign relations and defence, and since 1949 a Political Agent in Doha has advised the Ruler on everything from oil concessions to the police. The present Agent, the veteran Arabist Edward Henderson, presides over the final phase of the relationship after London's decision to withdraw from the Gulf by the end of 1971.

The Agency works to leave behind a stable, Western-friendly government: a federation with Bahrain and the Trucial States if possible, a modern administration under the Heir Apparent, oil flowing through Western companies and no opening for Arab radicals or the Soviet Union. Its leverage is advice, intelligence, the oil companies and half a century of habitual deference.

1.name: Ahl al-Shura
1.text:
The Partisans of Consultation are Doha's established notables: heads of leading Qatari families, prosperous merchants, qadis and senior officials who gather in one another's majlises and expect to be heard. They watched the unrest of 1963 with alarm, but they also resent rule by decree, the extravagance of the ruling family and the Ruler's long absences abroad.

They want an orderly modern state on conservative lines: a written basic law, an appointed consultative council of notables, an end to arbitrary privileges and close ties with Britain and Saudi Arabia. They reject parties, strikes and revolutionary slogans. Their leverage is social standing and the ear of the Heir Apparent, who needs their support for his reforms.

2.name: Jil al-Bi'that
2.text:
The Scholarship Generation are the young Qataris sent abroad on government scholarships since the late 1950s, now returning from Cairo, Beirut, Baghdad, Kuwait and Britain as teachers, engineers, doctors and administrators. They are few in number but staff the expanding government departments and the oil sector, and they meet in clubs, offices and the majlises of reform-minded shaikhs.

They want a constitution with real rights, a civil service based on merit, Qatarisation of posts held by expatriates, a free press and public money spent on education and health rather than family allowances. Most admire Arab nationalism but prefer reform to revolution. Their leverage is indispensability: a growing state cannot be run without them.

3.name: 'Ummal Dukhan
3.text:
The Dukhan Workers are the Qatari, Arab and Iranian employees of the Qatar Petroleum Company's oilfield at Dukhan and its terminal at Umm Said, together with the workforce of Shell's offshore operation. Their strikes of the 1950s and of 1963 won better pay and housing, but trade unions remain forbidden and organisers risk dismissal or deportation.

They demand a legal right to organise, fair wages, priority for Qatari nationals, safe working conditions and pensions, and believe a labour law on the Kuwaiti or British model can be won without revolution. Politically they lean towards Arab nationalism but keep to bread-and-butter demands. Their leverage is simple: Qatar's entire income flows through the pipelines they operate.

4.name: Ansar al-Salam
4.text:
The Peace Partisans are a small circle of Moscow-line communists among Qatar's expatriate workforce, mainly Iraqi, Bahraini and Palestinian clerks, teachers and oil technicians, who take their name from the Soviet-backed peace movement of the Arab East. They keep in touch with Bahrain's National Liberation Front and the Iraqi Communist Party and work in strict secrecy.

They circulate literature on the Soviet Union, anti-imperialist solidarity and workers' rights, and call for nationalisation of oil, an end to British protection and friendship with the socialist camp. Any member who is exposed faces immediate deportation. Their leverage is slight but real: a network inside the oil company and the schools that can turn grievances into organisation.

5.name: Harakat al-Qawmiyyin al-'Arab
5.text:
The Arab Nationalist Movement, founded by George Habash and his comrades in Beirut in the early 1950s, found a following in Qatar among teachers, clerks and students during the Nasserist upsurge of the late 1950s and early 1960s. Since the movement's turn to Marxism and the break-up of its regional branches in 1968-69, its Qatari circles are small, clandestine and divided.

Its radical wing calls for armed struggle against the shaikhs and the British, solidarity with the Dhofar revolution and the Palestinian fedayeen, and a socialist Arab Gulf. Older Nasserist members prefer agitation and education. Its leverage lies in youth and school networks and in links to comrades in Kuwait, Bahrain and Aden.

6.name: Ri'asat al-Mahakim al-Shar'iyya
6.text:
The Presidency of the Shari'a Courts is the summit of Qatar's religious establishment and, so far, its only real judiciary. For three decades it has been led by Shaikh Abdullah bin Zaid Al Mahmoud, a Hanbali scholar of great authority who also oversees religious affairs and the Quranic schools.

The qadis around him resist secular codes and civil courts, Western-style entertainment, alcohol for expatriates and the influence of foreign teachers, and insist that any constitution must make Shari'a supreme. They are wary of every imported ideology, Western liberalism and Arab socialism alike. Their leverage is religious legitimacy: no ruler of Wahhabi Qatar can openly defy them.

7.name: Al-Nasiriyyun
7.text:
Gamal Abdel Nasser's broadcasts and Egypt's teachers made Qatar's youth passionate Arab nationalists in the late 1950s, and in April 1963 their celebration of Arab unity ended in gunfire and a general strike. The Nasserists have no organisation today, but the sentiment survives among civil servants, students and the Egyptian and Palestinian staff of the schools.

They want Qatar inside a strong Arab bloc led from Cairo, free of British tutelage, with oil wealth used for Arab causes and a centralised, army-backed modernising state in place of shaikhly rule. They regard the Soviet Union as a useful friend and America as Israel's protector. Their leverage is the emotional power of Nasser's name in moments of Arab crisis.

8.name: Al-Shiraziyyun
8.text:
The Shirazis are the followers in Qatar of Grand Ayatollah Muhammad al-Shirazi of Karbala, whose representatives collect religious dues and organise study circles among the country's Shia minority of Baharna and Iranian origin. They gather in the husayniyyas of Doha, where young men are taught to see faith as a call to action.

They seek dignity and equal treatment for Qatar's Shia, freedom to hold their rituals and build their own religious institutions, and a society governed by Islamic values under the guidance of the clergy. For now they avoid confrontation with the Al Thani. Their leverage lies in the community's merchant wealth and in the Shirazi network of clerics spanning Iraq, Kuwait and the Gulf.

9.name: Muqallidu al-Khumayni
9.text:
Khomeini's Followers are a small circle of Qatari and Iranian-born Shia who take Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, exiled in Najaf since 1965, as their source of emulation. They pass around his writings and rulings and send their religious dues to his representatives, keeping well away from the attention of the police and of Iran's SAVAK.

They regard the Shah as a tyrant and a servant of America and Israel, and hold that the clergy must take charge of Muslim government rather than leave it to kings. In Qatar they are quiet, but their loyalty runs to Najaf, not Doha. Their leverage lies in fervour and in their contacts with Khomeini's networks across Iraq, Kuwait and Iran.

10.name: Al Thani
10.text:
The Al Thani have led Qatar since the mid-nineteenth century, when Muhammad bin Thani and his son Jassim united the peninsula's tribes. The Ruler, Shaikh Ahmad bin Ali Al Thani, has reigned since 1960 but spends long periods abroad, leaving his cousin and Heir Apparent, Shaikh Khalifa bin Hamad, to run the government. Britain still handles defence and foreign affairs.

The family rules as a Wahhabi monarchy in close alliance with Saudi Arabia, relying on Shari'a, tribal consensus and oil revenues, a large share of which goes in allowances to its hundreds of shaikhs. It wants independence on its own terms, a Gulf federation that does not subordinate Doha, and no parties. Its leverage is oil money, the police and the loyalty of the tribes.

11.name: Hizb al-Tahrir
11.text:
Hizb ut-Tahrir, the Party of Liberation founded in Jerusalem in 1953 by Taqi al-Din al-Nabhani, has carried its call for a restored caliphate to the Gulf through Jordanian and Palestinian teachers and clerks. In Qatar its secret study circles reach into schools, government offices and mosques, and its leaflets denounce the shaikhs, the British and the nationalists alike.

The party holds that every existing Muslim state is un-Islamic and that one caliph must unite the umma under Shari'a once power is handed over by those who hold it, above all military officers. It rejects democracy, socialism and both superpowers. Its leverage lies in a disciplined, educated membership and the appeal of a pure ideal to pious youth.

12.name: Al-Ikhwan al-Muslimun
12.text:
The Muslim Brotherhood has no formal branch in Qatar, but its influence runs deep through the Egyptian scholars and teachers who escaped Nasser's prisons and found refuge in Doha. Most prominent among them is Shaikh Yusuf al-Qaradawi, director of the Religious Institute since 1961, whose sermons and lessons have made him the country's best-known preacher.

The Brothers seek Islamic renewal through education, preaching and the training of a pious, modern-educated generation, and want the new state's schools, courts and media to reflect Islamic values. They oppose Nasserism, communism and Western secularism alike. Their leverage lies in the classrooms they shape and in their access to the Heir Apparent and the education department.

13.name: Rijal Wali al-'Ahd
13.text:
The Heir Apparent's Men are the officials, advisers and loyal shaikhs gathered around Shaikh Khalifa bin Hamad Al Thani, Deputy Ruler since 1960 and the real head of Qatar's administration while the Ruler is abroad. Khalifa controls the finances and oil revenues and is preparing a provisional constitution and a council of ministers that he expects to lead.

They stand for a modern centralised state: budgets, ministries, planning, schools and hospitals, a curb on the family's spending and a cautious foreign policy balancing Britain, Saudi Arabia and the Arab world. They see consultation as useful but politics as dangerous. Their leverage is control of the treasury and the bureaucracy, and the general expectation that the future belongs to Khalifa.

14.name: Shuyukh al-Badiya
14.text:
The Shaikhs of the Desert are the chiefs of Qatar's Bedouin and semi-settled tribes, among them the Bani Hajir, Al Murrah and Al Na'im, whose kinsmen live on both sides of the Saudi border; the Na'im also figure in Bahrain's old claim to Zubara. Many of their young men now serve in the police or work in the oilfields, but tribal loyalty and customary law still govern their lives.

They expect the Al Thani to honour the old compact: subsidies, land, wells, jobs and respect for tribal custom in return for loyalty. They distrust city reformers, foreign ideas and anything that would reduce the shaikhs' authority over their people. Their leverage lies in manpower, in ties to Saudi Arabia and in the dynasty's need for tribal backing in every succession.

15.name: Ghurfat Tijarat Qatar
15.text:
The Qatar Chamber of Commerce, established in 1963, speaks for Doha's merchant houses, such as the Al Mana, Darwish, Al Fardan and Jaidah families, which hold the agencies for Western cars, machinery and consumer goods and win the contracts of the oil boom. Its leading members are tied to the ruling family through partnerships and patronage.

The Chamber wants contracts, agencies and licences reserved for Qatari nationals, a sound Qatar-Dubai riyal, public works financed by oil and friendly relations with Britain and the West. It fears both nationalisation and the radicals of 1963. Its leverage is capital, credit and the fact that much of the state's spending passes through its members' hands.

16.name: Tujjar Suq Waqif
16.text:
The Suq Waqif Traders are the shopkeepers, wholesalers, money changers and dhow importers of Doha's old market and the streets around it, a mix of Qataris, Iranians, Indians and other Arabs. Smaller than the great merchant houses, they live from re-export trade, retail and the spending of a fast-growing town of immigrants.

They want low duties, few licences, easy credit and the freedom to import and sell without the monopolies of the big agency holders or the controls of planners. They are wary of both radical politics and an overbearing state. Their leverage lies in daily commerce: when the suq closes its shutters, all of Doha notices.

17.name: Humat al-Maha
17.text:
The Guardians of the Oryx are falconers, hunters and lovers of the desert among the shaikhs and tribesmen who have watched motorised hunting parties strip the peninsula of its gazelles, houbara bustards and Arabian oryx within a single generation. Some prominent shaikhs have begun keeping captive herds of oryx and gazelle to save the animals from extinction.

They call for limits on hunting with cars and rifles, protected grazing areas, care for the desert's scarce wells and vegetation, and respect for traditional falconry, which depends on healthy wild stocks. Their concern is heritage more than ideology. Their leverage is the personal passion of influential shaikhs for the desert and its creatures.

18.name: Harakat al-Tahrir al-Watani al-Filastini
18.text:
Fatah has deep roots in Qatar, where Palestinian civil servants and teachers, among them Mahmoud Abbas and Muhammad Yusuf al-Najjar, built one of its earliest branches in the late 1950s and 1960s. Since the battle of Karameh in 1968 its prestige has soared, and Palestinians in Doha's departments, schools and oil companies give part of their salaries to the revolution.

The movement stands for the liberation of Palestine through armed struggle, independent of the Arab regimes, and keeps out of Qatari politics in return for official tolerance and donations. Its outlook is non-aligned and broadly progressive, open to aid from East and West alike. Its leverage lies in the size and skills of the Palestinian community and the sympathy its fedayeen command.

19.name: Al-Jabha al-Sha'biyya li-Tahrir al-Khalij al-'Arabi al-Muhtall
19.english: Popular Front for the Liberation of the Occupied Arab Gulf
19.native_full: Al-Jabha al-Sha'biyya li-Tahrir al-Khalij al-'Arabi al-Muhtall
19.text:
The Popular Front for the Liberation of the Occupied Arab Gulf, born of the Dhofar rebellion and renamed at its Hamrin congress in 1968, claims Qatar as part of the Gulf it intends to liberate. Its Qatari following is a handful of radicalised students and expatriate sympathisers who smuggle its literature and collect money for the guerrillas in southern Oman.

The Front calls for people's war against the shaikhs, the British and the oil companies, and for a single socialist republic of the Gulf. It draws inspiration from Mao, receives Chinese and South Yemeni support and despises the federation plans as a colonial device. Its leverage in Qatar is limited, but the Dhofar guerrillas' successes lend it glamour among the young.
19.wiki: Popular Front for the Liberation of Oman

20.name: Jabhat al-Wahda al-Wataniyya
20.text:
The National Unity Front emerged in April 1963, when a member of the ruling family fired on a crowd celebrating Arab unity and the killing set off a general strike. Its petition demanded curbs on Al Thani privileges, jobs for Qataris before foreigners, social services and municipal councils. The Ruler crushed it within weeks and its leaders were jailed or exiled; it survives as a banned memory and a circle of veterans.

Its populism combines Arab nationalism with resentment of shaikhly arrogance and of foreign labour. It demands justice for ordinary Qataris, a fair share of the oil wealth and limits on immigration. Its leverage is the grievance it still embodies and the memory of the one moment ordinary Qataris defied the regime.

21.name: Hizb al-Ba'th al-'Arabi al-Ishtiraki
21.text:
Ba'athist cells have existed in Qatar since the 1950s among Iraqi, Syrian, Palestinian and Jordanian teachers and a few Qatari students who met the party abroad. Since the split of 1966 most look to the Iraqi leadership that seized power in Baghdad in July 1968, and they work quietly to avoid deportation.

The party preaches Arab unity, freedom and socialism under a vanguard party, the end of British protection and of the shaikhdoms as separate states, and the use of Gulf oil for the Arab nation. It is hostile to Iran, to Zionism and to the conservative monarchies. Its leverage lies in Iraqi patronage, scholarships and propaganda, and in its foothold in the teaching profession.

22.name: Quwwat al-Amn al-'Amm
22.text:
Qatar has no regular army yet; its armed power is the Public Security force, the police and mobile units raised since 1949 and expanded with oil revenues, still commanded in part by British contract officers. Its ranks include Qataris, Bedouin tribesmen and Arabs from neighbouring countries, and it answers directly to the Al Thani.

Its officers aim to become the core of a national army when Britain leaves, and they want modern weapons, better pay and a share of influence. They have no ideology beyond loyalty to the dynasty and fear of subversion. Their leverage lies in being the only organised armed force in the country, a fact no branch of the ruling family can ignore.

23.name: Ahl al-Mukhassasat
23.text:
The Allowance Shaikhs are the hundreds of male Al Thani who draw monthly stipends, land and privileges from the oil revenues, which together with the Ruler's privy purse absorb a large share of state income. Many of the most powerful belong to the Ruler's own branch, and they look to Shaikh Ahmad bin Ali to protect their share against the Heir Apparent's budget-cutting.

They see Qatar as the family's patrimony: the ruling house should hold the land, the offices and the wealth, with no constitution limiting its rights and no accounting to commoners. They distrust reformers and radicals alike. Their leverage lies in their numbers, arms and tribal ties, and in the dynasty's fear of a family revolt.
